author: Alex Nieves
title: California's emissions authority is cracking - NewsBreak
text:
By Alex Nieves ,
5 hours ago With help from Noah Baustin, Camille von Kaenel and Marisa Guerra Echeverria
DEATH BY 1,000 CUTS: Republicans have steadily picked away at California’s authority to slash vehicle emissions since President Donald Trump returned to office.
Democrats are now afraid they’ve finally found a way to undermine it for good.
When the House returns from its summer recess on Thursday, conservative lawmakers will have the chance to move a half-dozen resolutions that would revoke EPA waivers granted to California under the Biden and Obama administrations (those waivers are the magic ticket that allows the state to enforce stricter-than-federal emissions standards for cars, trucks, and ships).
The Republicans’ bevy of resolutions is part of a larger effort to use the Congressional Review Act — a 1996 law that gives Congress the power to revoke agency rules — to undermine Democrats’ policy agendas.
Trump already used the CRA process to kill three of California’s waivers last year, including the state’s controversial zero-emissions sales mandates for passenger cars and commercial trucks.
Without the power to set its own emissions standards, California’s ambitious climate goals will realistically be out of reach. That also means California can’t meet air quality standards for pollutants like nitrogen oxides — a main component of smog — required under federal law, and could face penalties.
“They’re making it more difficult to comply with the Clean Air Act, which potentially could lead to sanctions,” said former California Air Resources Board Chair Liane Randolph . “It’s clearly a political power play to attack even the most basic environmental protections.”
Unlike those electric vehicle rules that Trump targeted last year, which roughly a dozen other states followed and had significant power to transform the vehicle market, the California standards now in question are, in some cases, decades old, and have largely already been complied with.
Legal thinkers on both sides of the partisan spectrum say Republicans’ larger strategy is to make it harder for state regulators to use Section 209 of the Clean Air Act, a carveout in the nearly 60-year-old federal law that allows California — which routinely has the nation’s worst air quality — to enforce stricter emissions standards.
That’s because the Congressional Review Act bars agencies from instituting new rules that are “substantially the same” as those that have already been revoked. (What exactly “substantially the same” means is currently the subject of a court case.)
“California’s climate zealots have run roughshod over the rest of the country for too long,” Wyoming Sen. Cynthia Lummis said in a statement after introducing a resolution earlier this month. “I’m proud to lead this fight to reclaim Congress’s authority and stop California from legislating for the entire nation.”
Even if Republicans are unlikely to have the votes to amend the Clean Air Act itself, the threat that any rule California comes up with in the future will eventually be “CRA-d” could force state regulators back to the drawing board.
“It’s a death by 1,000 cuts sort of deal,” said Michael Buschbacher , an attorney who represents ethanol and fossil fuel interests, along with vehicle dealers. “I think the goal here is to limit the options list for California.”
Whether lawmakers will vote on the latest round of resolutions is an open question, as Republicans face a heavy workload through the end of the year, and a midterm election in which Democrats have a real chance of retaking the House or Senate.
But California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued the EPA for sending the waivers to Congress for review in the first place, hoping a court will find they aren’t rules lawmakers can vote to revoke.
Senate Parliamentarian Elizabeth MacDonough — who acts as the chamber’s procedural adviser — told lawmakers last year that the waivers aren’t considered “rules” under the Congressional Review Act, advice Republican leaders ignored. (A federal judge appeared torn during arguments on California’s lawsuit in a hearing last week.)
State officials have largely been unwilling to talk about a scenario in which the courts uphold Republicans’ maneuver, and what the state’s strategy would look like if that happens. “We remain confident in our ability to prevail in court,” CARB Chair Lauren Sanchez said in an interview earlier this month.
But some former CARB officials say that California, and the Democratic Party more broadly, should already be rethinking their strategy.
Craig Segall , a former CARB deputy executive officer who is now a policy consultant, argued that the way California has developed emissions standards for decades is “pretty close to irreparably damaged,” and said he’s not hopeful that the Supreme Court will find Republicans’ tactics illegal, even if lower courts say the CRA was used improperly.
Democrats in California and D.C. should focus on bolstering domestic production of technologies like electric vehicles and batteries instead, he said, pointing to pieces of President Joe Biden ’s Inflation Reduction Act, like manufacturing incentives, that survived Trump’s rollbacks.
Randolph, however, argued that Section 209 — California’s exemption from the Clean Air Act — ultimately still exists, and that California should not concede its power. “The state should continue to defend that authority and implement that authority,” she said. — AN

CRUNCH TIME: There are less than three days left for lawmakers to introduce a bill with the blockbuster wildfire liability package that Gov. Gavin Newsom is pushing for. The governor is getting testy.
A reporter asked Newsom on Wednesday what he made of the Senate’s counter proposal , which would ax one of his key priorities: prohibiting insurance companies from recouping wildfire losses from utilities that spark blazes, a process called subrogation.
“If you’re with the insurance companies and you think they should be paid before victims, OK, that’s a point of view, I’m not going to defend that,” Newsom said.
Despite the snark, the governor said that he thought that his team was gaining ground.
“I think we’re making progress and we have some additional ideas, we’re creative,” Newsom said. “It’s part of my day today, tomorrow, and my Friday and Saturday, Sunday.”
It’s clear that Newsom feels the clock ticking, though. “I just wish I had a little, few more months here,” he said.
That prompted questions about whether the governor would call for a special legislative session on the matter. “We’ll see how life unfolds, there’s a lot of time between now and that 72-hour rule,” Newsom said. — NB
MAILBOX: Meanwhile, wildfire liability is the talk of the town in Sacramento, and powerful interest groups across the state are staking out positions while the final terms of a deal remain in flux.
That includes the ratepayer advocacy group, The Utility Reform Network, which sent a Tuesday letter to Newsom and legislative leaders detailing its priorities. If the state does place a $6 billion per fire cap on withdrawals from the wildfire fund that backstops utilities when they spark blazes, lawmakers should have state emergency funds cover the next $2 billion after the cap to ease the burden on electricity customers, the group argued.
And on Monday, the California Professional Firefighters organization, which represents first responders statewide, sent a letter to Newsom backing his wildfire liability proposal. The organization appreciates “adjustments to ensure that local governments are not unduly impacted” by wildfires, noting the importance of governments getting rebuilding funds.
That may signal movement from the governor’s office on one of its most controversial recommendations: barring local governments from recovering the full replacement cost of infrastructure from utilities that cause wildfires.
Insurance company CEOs are also getting in the mix. Fifteen of them, including giants like State Farm, signed a letter to legislative leaders on Wednesday warning that eliminating or reducing their ability to recoup some wildfire losses from utilities would force them to raise premiums and possibly pull back out of offering coverage to risky fire-prone areas. — NB, CvK
NITTY GRITTY: Last but not least, POLITICO obtained a copy of the Assembly wildfire liability working group caucus update from Friday.
It contains a few key nuggets that didn’t make it into the version of its proposal that detailed priority talking points.
For example, it specifies that it would be electricity customers who cover utility costs above the $6 billion per-fire cap they’re proposing placing on the wildfire fund (shareholders would have to pay the money back if the utility was found to have acted imprudently).
Also, while the Assembly wants to reject Newsom’s proposal to cap local government economic damage claims, it does want to limit corporate claims for property loss.
Finally, the document mentions codifying Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara ’s recent package of rules meant to entice insurance companies back to the state by letting them raise rates to reflect the growing costs of both climate change and reinsurance, known as the “Sustainable Insurance Strategy.” — NB, CvK
ON TO THE GOVERNOR’S DESK: State lawmakers may still be in the thick of negotiations on hot topics like wildfire liability and climate funding, but they’re also taking final votes on hundreds of other bills and sending them to Newsom to sign, veto or become law without his signature by the Sept. 30 deadline.
Among them:
AB 2589 , a bill by Assemblymember Jacqui Irwin . The Assembly voted to concur with the Senate’s amendments on this measure on Wednesday, sending it to Newsom’s desk. It aims to ensure that any money that Pacific Gas & Electric, Southern California Edison and San Diego Gas & Electric save as a result of the corporate tax cuts put in place by President Donald Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act is refunded to electricity customers and not kept as profits for the companies.
AB 2463 , a bill by Assemblymember Cottie Petrie-Norris . The Assembly also concurred in the amendments on this measure on Wednesday, which would require the California Public Utilities Commission to conduct its own analysis of the appropriate profit rates it sets for the investor-owned utilities, a response to electricity customer advocate concerns that the existing process is too opaque.
AB 2218 , a bill by Assemblymember Ash Kalra to bolster requirements that state water regulators consult with tribes, as well as establish a new mediation system for disputes. The bill was opposed by business groups and water agencies, which are still fighting a different tribal water bill, AB 1881 , by Assemblymember James Ramos .
SB 1135 , a bill by Sen. Catherine Blakespear to reestablish a statewide program promoting coexistence with wildlife like mountain lions, as well as codify a program compensating ranchers for losses of livestock to wolves. Still missing, though: reliable funding.
SB 925 , a bill by Sen. Jerry McNerney to require the California Energy Commission develop a strategic plan to advance fusion energy.
SB 1283 , a bill by Sen. Angelique Ashby that requires cities and counties to update their ordinances to speed up permitting for electric vehicle charger projects. — NB, CvK, AN
SOME BREATHING ROOM: California’s carbon market posted its strongest auction results in more than two years on Wednesday, giving Newsom and the California Air Resources Board a bit of a political reprieve. Some lawmakers had criticized the agency’s decision to overhaul the carbon market’s rules to make it easier for businesses to comply, a decision which threatened future revenue.
Permit prices rose to $32.48 per ton of carbon, the highest since May 2024, and all current-year allowances sold. The auction generated roughly $870 million for state coffers.
But one strong auction won’t settle the broader fight about climate funding in Sacramento, with lawmakers still negotiating how to bridge a multi-billion-dollar gap this year between the programs they promised to fund with revenues from the market and the money the market is expected to produce overall.
The next few years are even murkier: The carbon market changes are set to take formal effect next month, and the most controversial change, which would offer incentives to companies that spend on emissions reduction technologies, isn’t set to fully land until next year. — CvK
SPEAKING OF CARBON: A coalition of over 80 transit, housing and labor groups is backing a Senate proposal to boost funding for programs supported by carbon market revenues, but wants more money for affordable housing.
The group of more than 80 organizations sent a letter to Gov. Newsom and legislative leaders expressing support for most of the plan, released last week, to provide an additional $500 million for climate programs this budget year. But the letter, shared exclusively with POLITICO, said a final agreement must include more money for affordable housing.
The Senate’s proposal would provide $278 million for the Affordable Housing and Sustainable Communities program, though lawmakers had agreed on a max of $840 million when they renegotiated the state’s cap-and-invest program last year.
“While we applaud the proposal’s investments in transit and environmental justice programs, a comprehensive final deal must address voters’ top concern: housing affordability,” said Chione Lucina Muñoz Flegal , executive director of Housing California.
It’s still unclear if Newsom’s office and Assembly leaders will come to the table to hash out a deal. Coalition leaders with knowledge of negotiations said the Senate’s proposal was met with a cold response in the Assembly. — AN
FIRST IN CURRENTS: San Francisco is launching a new effort to build curbside electric vehicle chargers for renters and people who live in multifamily homes without access to a private garage.
The program, which kicked off Wednesday, aims to install 100 curbside charging stations across San Francisco by 2030. The effort follows a pilot program the city launched in 2024 to gather data on site selection, coordination with utility companies and permitting hurdles.
“This program is a commonsense way to make it easier for San Franciscans to own an electric vehicle and help us achieve our climate goals together,” said San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie in a statement. “Curbside charging will help families save money and do their part to improve air quality — making our city more affordable, more resilient, and cleaner.”
Auto market experts and car companies argue that the lack of access to convenient charging for the millions of California drivers who live in multifamily dwellings, like apartments, remains one of the biggest hurdles to EV growth in the state. Electric vehicles represent roughly 20 percent of new car sales in California, but the percentage has been dropping in recent years. — AN
— Los Angeles renters are protesting soaring utility bills that are calculated by third-party, formula-based systems.
— The California Chamber of Commerce has spearheaded an effort to oppose a bill that would give Native American communities broader say over their ancestral lands .
— Scientists have recorded the highest temperature measured in the world’s oceans, a feat compounded by El Niño conditions.
